extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning elementary combinatorics and probability (advanced high-school / undergraduate / general readers of 'The Principles of Science')
extracted.subtask_description: Expository guidance on counting permutations and combinations: distinguishing when order matters, computing factorials, handling indistinguishable items, using the arithmetical (Pascal) triangle, and applying these counts to probability and enumerative problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of natural phenomena are restricted by prior conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all logically possible combinations actually occur in nature; the set of realizable events is limited by physical/biological/linguistic constraints and it is the work of science to discover those restricting conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: English words cannot use arbitrary letter sequences due to vocal-organ constraints (vowels required, limits on consonant clusters); scientific inquiry must investigate which combinations are possible rather than assume all logical combinations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between combinations and permutations (order-sensitivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permutation: order matters (treat AB different from BA). Combination: only presence/absence matters, order is ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: letters a,e,m,n form one combination but many permutations; gunpowder components indifferent to order (combination) while mechanical operations or sequences of events often require permutations (specific order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting permutations of n distinct things: n! rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are n distinct items, the number of permutations (arrangements) is n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 1, commonly denoted n! (factorial of n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 3 letters A,B,C → 3×2×1 = 6 permutations; 4 letters → 4×3×2×1 = 24; ordering days of the week → 7! = 5040 (excluding existing order gives 5039).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of factorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorial n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n; factorials grow extremely rapidly and are used repeatedly in permutation/combination formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and table: 4! = 24, 5! = 120, 6! = 720, ...; factorials up to 12 listed; factorials are used to compute permutations and combinations and appear in many analytic formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutations with indistinguishable/repeated items: divide by factorials of repeats
rubrics_metrics.description: When some items are identical, compute permutations as if all distinct (n!), then divide by the factorial of the multiplicity of each set of identical items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ANN (3 letters with two identical n's): 3! / 2! = 3 distinct orders; UTILITARIANISM (14 letters with four i's, two a's, two t's): 14!/(4!2!2!) = 908,107,200; Mississippi yields 34,650 permutations by similar division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting combinations by dividing permutations by number of orderings (combination formula via permutations)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count combinations of m items chosen from n without regard to order, compute the ordered selections (n × (n−1) × ... × (n−m+1)) and divide by m! to remove permutations of each chosen set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: choose 3 letters from 26 without repetition: (26×25×24)/3! = 2600 combinations. For selecting a committee of 5 from 30: (30×29×28×27×26)/(5!) = 142,506.

rubrics_metrics.name: General combination formula (binomial coefficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of ways to choose m things out of n is given by the formula n·(n−1)·(n−2)·...·(n−m+1) divided by m!, equivalently n!/(m!(n−m)!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formula recurs throughout combinations and probability problems; historically attributed to Pascal/De Gua/others and appears in many analytic expansions (binomial theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical (Pascal's) Triangle: construction by successive additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the triangle starting with 1 at the apex; each subsequent line is formed by shifting the previous line one place right and adding corresponding entries. The triangle is symmetric and infinite in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example lines: 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1; 1 4 6 4 1; etc. The triangle organizes binomial coefficients and figurate numbers and serves as a ready table of combination counts for many n and m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Columns of the triangle correspond to figurate numbers and difference relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Columns of the triangle yield sequences like units, natural numbers, triangular numbers, pyramidal numbers, etc.; differences between columns reflect lower-column sequences (first differences, second differences, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangular numbers (1,3,6,10,15...) appear in the third column; pyramidal numbers in the fourth; the triangle classifies numbers by which order of difference equals unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row sums and cumulative sums: powers of two and 2^n − 1 identities
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of numbers in the nth horizontal line of the arithmetical triangle is 2^(n−1). The sum of the first n lines is 2^n − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus successive row sums: 1,2,4,8,16,... ; and cumulative sums equal one less than powers of two. This mirrors the counts of logical combinations (logical alphabet columns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the triangle to look up combination counts (indexing rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the number of combinations of m things out of n, look in the (n+1)th line of the triangle and take the (m+1)th entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: combinations of 3 out of 7 appear as the fourth number in the 8th line; sub-committee of 5 out of 9 → sixth number in the 10th line = 126.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficients and link to binomial theorem / logical alphabet
rubrics_metrics.description: Each column of the logical alphabet corresponds to binomial coefficients in the arithmetical triangle; summing logical combinations yields the triangle entries and demonstrates simple cases of the binomial theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for four letters A,B,C,D the counts of selections with 4,3,2,1,0 positives are 1,4,6,4,1 (fifth line). The identity between summing combinations by size and powers of two underlies binomial expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of combinatorial counts to probability and distributions (binomial distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binomial coefficients from the triangle give the number of equally possible cases for counts of successes (e.g., heads) in repeated independent trials; these counts underpin probability calculations and frequency-of-divergence analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with 4 coin tosses, counts of 0..4 heads are 1,4,6,4,1 out of 16 total cases; the triangle is used to derive probabilities and to study distributions of deviations from an average (Quetelet, Galton references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical enumeration examples and applications (planet conjunctions, organ stops, language permutations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorics is applied to enumerate real-world possibilities: conjunctions of planets, ways to draw organ stops, arrangements of letters/words, and estimating the immense variety of possibilities in nature and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: conjunctions of 8 planets counted by summing combination counts for 2..8 give 247 possible conjunctions (excluding empty and single-planet cases); an organ with 11 stops has 2048 draw combinations including none.
